coredata.dc:description: A lipolytic enzyme (Rcut) was discovered from the Rhodococcusstrain (RosL12) isolated from the Antarctic Ross Sea. The corresponding gene composed of 651 bases encoding 216 amino acids. It was found to be a cutinase gene through BLAST search. Rcut has a signal sequence consisting of 29 amino acids. An active Rcut was produced after the intact gene containing the signal sequence was transformed into Escherichia coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS. Rcut was purified through a nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid purification system and a carboxymethyl Sepharose column chromatography. Its specific activity was 2190 U/mg. Rcut showed the highest activity at 40 °C and had a low activation energy of 3.16 kcal/mol. This means that it is a typical cold-adapted enzyme. Rcut showed high activity towards medium chain fatty acids (C4–C10). Rcut degraded polycaprolactone and polyethylene terephthalate, suggesting that it could be used for decomposition of synthetic plastics causing environmental pollution. Rcut was immobilized on methacrylate-divinyl benzene bead. This immobilized Rcut (immRcut) showed higher thermal stability than the free enzyme. ImmRcut performed transesterification of various esters and ethanol in a non-polar solvent, suggesting that it could be used for the synthesis of industrially useful ester compounds.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: A lipolytic enzyme (Rcut) was discovered from the Rhodococcusstrain (RosL12) isolated from the Antarctic Ross Sea. The corresponding gene composed of 651 bases encoding 216 amino acids. It was found to be a cutinase gene through BLAST search. Rcut has a signal sequence consisting of 29 amino acids. An active Rcut was produced after the intact gene containing the signal sequence was transformed into Escherichia coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS. Rcut was purified through a nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid purification system and a carboxymethyl Sepharose column chromatography. Its specific activity was 2190 U/mg. Rcut showed the highest activity at 40 °C and had a low activation energy of 3.16 kcal/mol. This means that it is a typical cold-adapted enzyme. Rcut showed high activity towards medium chain fatty acids (C4–C10). Rcut degraded polycaprolactone and polyethylene terephthalate, suggesting that it could be used for decomposition of synthetic plastics causing environmental pollution. Rcut was immobilized on methacrylate-divinyl benzene bead. This immobilized Rcut (immRcut) showed higher thermal stability than the free enzyme. ImmRcut performed transesterification of various esters and ethanol in a non-polar solvent, suggesting that it could be used for the synthesis of industrially useful ester compounds.

ce:section.ce:para: The marine environment has many unusual places with special conditions such as extreme temperature, pH, salt concentration, and pressure [1]. Some enzymes obtained from marine microorganisms have the property of not losing their enzyme activities even under harsh conditions. Thus, they are of great research and practical value [2]. Accordingly, these enzymes have been frequently applied in various industrial fields such as food, textiles, cleaning, environment, and medicine [3].

Cutinases (EC 3.1.1.74) produced by some fungi and bacteria can decompose cutin present in plants [4]. Cutin exists as an outer layer at the tip of all terrestrial plants. It has a very hydrophobic property. Cutin is mainly composed of 16 and 18 carbons that can form ester bonds with each other. Some fungi and bacteria express cutinase to penetrate into plants [5]. Some parasitic microorganisms can also produce cutinase to use cutin as a carbon source [6].

Cutinase is an enzyme hydrolyzing triglycerides containing ester bonds without exhibiting the 'interfacial activation' phenomena shown in most lipases [7]. Cutinase is an efficient enzyme for decomposing triglycerides because it does not have a hydrophobic lid part that is commonly observed in lipases. Thus, it is easy for its active site to access natural polymers such as cutin and synthetic polymers [8]. Most cutinases have catalytic triads composed of Ser, His, and Asp, like other serine hydrolases [9].

Cutinase belongs to the smallest α/β hydrolase family. It is an enzyme capable of not only hydrolysis, but also esterification and transesterification [5]. This ability suggests that this enzyme has the potential to be used in various industrial fields. In the food industry, cutinase has been used for the production of dehydrated fruits, dairy products, flavoring compounds, and some fatty acids [10]. In the detergent industry, cutinase has been used in the washing process because cutinase has stability in the pH range of 8–11 and in the temperature range of 20–50 °C, even in the presence of hydrogen peroxide [10]. In the chemical industry, cutinase is used in the production of biodiesel, phenolic compounds, surfactants, and some chiral chemicals. It has potential for functionalization of polymer surfaces as well as polymer recycling and coating removal [11–14]. In the environmental industry, cutinase can degrade wastes and pesticides composed of polymers in a mild condition [15]. In recent years, cutinase plays an important role as a biocatalyst in the textile industry [16]. As such, cutinase can reduce environmental pollution and the quality deterioration of cotton that occurs in the process of removing cuticles around cotton [5].
In the present study, a cutinase was obtained from a marine microorganism Rhodococcus sp. It was then purified to investigate its enzymatic properties.

Taq DNA polymerase, NdeI, EcoRI, and T4 DNA ligase were obtained from New England Biolabs, UK. Genomic DNA Prep Kit and pfu DNA polymerase were purchased from Solgent, Korea. Escherichia coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS was bought from Novagen, USA. Ni-NTA agarose affinity chromatography column was purchased from Qiagen, Germany. PD-10 column was obtained from GE Healthcare, USA. CM Sepharose column was supplied by Amersham Pharmacia Biotech, Sweden. Terephthalic acid (TPA), polycaprolactone (PCL), and polylactic acid (PLA) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, USA. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) film was bought from Goodfellow, UK. Bis (2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) was obtained from Tokyo chemical industry, JAPAN. Methacrylate-divinylbenzene (MA-DVB) resin was purchased from GenoFocus (Korea).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Cloning of a lipolytic gene from an Antarctic bacterial strain
ce:section.ce:para: The genomic DNA of the strain (RosL12) provided by the Korea Polar Research Institute was extracted using a Genomic DNA Prep Kit according to the manufacturer's instructions. 16S rDNA was made from the genomic DNA by PCR reaction using universal primers 27F and 1492R and Taq DNA polymerase. This PCR product was sequenced by Bionics (Seoul, Korea) using universal primers 518F and 800R (Supplementary Table S1). Using the nucleotide sequence (1405 bp), bacterial identification was done with the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) at the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/).

Rhodococcus genomic DNA was digested using EcoRI. The pUC19 plasmid was digested with the same enzyme and treated with calf intestinal alkaline phosphatase (CIAP) and mixed with genomic DNA fragments for ligation using T4 DNA ligase. The ligation mixture was transformed into E. coli DH5α and a recombinant E. coli colony showing lipolytic activity was isolated from Luria-Bertani (LB) agar medium containing tributyrin (1%). After culturing the recombinant E. coli in LB medium, the recombinant plasmid (pUC19-Rhod) was extracted using a Plasmid DNA Purification Kit (LaboPass, Korea) according to the manufacturer's instructions. By analyzing the nucleotide sequence of insert DNA, a gene (Rcut) predicted to encode a lipolytic enzyme was found.

Amino acid sequences of various cutinase enzymes deposited in PDB database (https://www.rcsb.org/) were aligned with the ClustalW method using MEGA 6.0 software (https://www.megasoftware.net/). A molecular phylogenetic tree was created using the Maximum Likelihood method based on aligned amino acid sequences.

3D homology modeling of Rcut protein was performed on the SWISS-MODEL server (https://swissmodel.expasy.org/). Fusarium solani cutinase (PDB: 1cex) was used as a template. The 3D structure was produced using PyMol software (https://pymol.org/).

Signal sequence prediction of Rcut protein was performed at SignalP 5.1 site (http://www.cbs.dtu.dk/services/SignalP/). Mutants (Δ17, Δ29) in which parts of the N-terminal signal sequence were removed from the wild type (WT) were prepared. In addition, those with and without C-terminal His-tag were prepared, respectively. Various primers (Supplementary Table S1) were used to produce these mutant enzymes. Each primer set and pUC19-Rhod plasmid were mixed and PCR was performed using pfu DNA polymerase. PCR products were digested using NdeI and XhoI. The pET22 vector was also digested with the same restriction enzymes, treated with CIAP, mixed with the insert DNA, and then subjected to ligation reaction using T4 DNA ligase. The ligation mixture was transformed into E. coli DH5α to obtain recombinant plasmids. To produce functional enzymes, the recombinant plasmid was transformed into E. coli BL21 (DE3) and E. coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS.

Cutinase was produced from E. coli BL21 (DE3) and Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS strains transformed with pET22 vector containing the wild type or mutant cutinase genes. After culturing each strain to an OD600nm of 0.6 in LB (200 ml) containing ampicillin (100 μM), 1 mM IPTG was added followed by culturing at 20 °C for another 16 h. In order to identify the newly expressed protein, E. coli BL21 (DE3) and E. coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS having the pET22 vector were also cultured in the same way. After collecting cells through centrifugation (6000×g for 10 min), the cell wet weight was measured to be 1.1 g for E. coli BL21 (DE3) and 0.36 g for E. coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS. Cells were resuspended using a 10 ml of lysis buffer (50 mM NaH2PO4, 300 mM NaCl, and 10 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). Cells were disrupted using an ultrasonicator and the supernatant (10 ml) was collected after centrifuging at 12,000×g for 10 min. Rcut protein was purified from the supernatant using a Ni-NTA agarose affinity chromatography column (3 ml volume). For washing, a washing buffer (50 mM NaH2PO4, 300 mM NaCl, and 20 mM imidazole, pH 8.0) was used. The washing step was performed twice using 10 ml of washing buffer. For elution of His-tagged Rcut, an elution buffer (50 mM NaH2PO4, 300 mM NaCl, and 500 mM imidazole, pH 8.0) was used. Elution was performed twice using 2 ml of elution buffer, and the elution solution was concentrated to 1 ml. The buffer was then changed to 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 6.5) using a PD-10 column. The protein was purified using a CM Sepharose column (0.5 ml) as follows. Protein was bound to the column using a 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 6.5). The protein was eluted from the column while increasing concentration of NaCl to 0.5 M in the same buffer (0.5 ml). Rcut was eluted with NaCl at a concentration of 0.3–0.4 M. The purity of the protein obtained through this process was confirmed through SDS-PAGE.

Enzyme activity assay was performed using p-nitrophenyl ester as a substrate. Then p-nitrophenol was measured at 405 nm absorbance. One unit of enzyme activity was defined as 1 μmol of p-nitrophenol released per min under standard assay conditions (pH 9.0, 30 °C). The enzyme reaction was performed in a 1 ml reaction mixture containing 950 μl of 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 9.0), 40 μl of ethanol, and 10 μl of 10 mM pNP-esters dissolved in acetonitrile. Enzyme activity was measured in triplicate. The average value was calculated.

The substrate specificity of this enzyme was measured using pNP-ester substrates having various chain lengths, including 10 mM pNP acetate (C2), pNP butyrate (C4), pNP caproate (C6), pNP caprylate (C8), pNP caprate (C10), pNP laurate (C12), pNP myristate (C14), pNP palmitate (C16), and pNP stearate (C18). These substrates were used to measure hydrolytic activities of the enzyme under standard analysis conditions.

The optimum temperature of this enzyme was measured in a Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0) using pNPC (C8) as a substrate at a temperature range of 0–60 °C for 10 min. To determine the thermal stability of this enzyme, it was treated at each temperature (20–50 °C) for 0–120 min. Its residual activity was then measured under standard analysis conditions.

The optimum pH of this enzyme was measured using 50 mM sodium citrate (pH 3.0–6.0), potassium phosphate (pH 6.0–8.0), Tris-HCl (pH 8.0–9.0), sodium carbonate-bicarbonate (pH 9.0–10.0), and sodium bicarbonate-NaOH (pH 10.0–11.0) buffers. For pH stability, the enzyme was reacted at room temperature for 1 h in each pH buffer. Its residual activity was then measured under standard analysis conditions.

The stability of the enzyme against organic solvents was determined by reacting the enzyme in various organic solvents at a concentration of 30% v/v at room temperature for 1 h. Its residual activity was then measured under standard analysis conditions.

Reactions with metal ions (5 mM), detergents (0.5%, v/v), and inhibitors (10 mM) were performed by reacting substances and the enzyme at room temperature for 1 h. The residual activity of the enzyme was then measured under standard analysis conditions.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Synthetic polyester degradation and scanning electron microscopy observation
ce:section.ce:para: Polycaprolactone (PCL) and polylactic acid (PLA) were dissolved in dichloromethane (DCM) at a concentration of 10% (v/v), respectively. The DCM solvent was evaporated at room temperature for 1 day to make PCL and PLA films. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) film was also used. After PCL was added to 10 ml of 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 9.0), 10 μl of enzyme (0.513 mg/ml) was added and the reaction was carried out at 30 °C for 6 h while rotating at 150 rpm. PLA and PET reacted with the enzyme for 24 h under the same conditions. After the enzymatic reaction, each material was washed with ethanol and water, dried completely, and the final weight was measured. The surface shape of each film was observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi, S-4800, Japan).

To confirm that the PET film was decomposed, the solution obtained by reacting PET and the enzyme was analyzed by HPLC. Cogent Bidentate C18 column (4.6 mm × 250 mm, 5 μm particle size; microSolv Technology Corp., Eatontown, NJ, USA) was used and 10 μl of the reaction solution was injected. The elution of the reaction solution was performed using a 23:77 ratio of solvent A (acetonitrile) and solvent B (0.5% phosphoric acid) at a flow rate of 1 ml/min at 25 °C. Decomposition products were detected at a UV wavelength of 250 nm.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Immobilization of Rcut using MA-DVB resin
ce:section.ce:para: MA-DVB resin (1 g) was reacted with methanol (10 ml) in a 30 ml size vial while rotating the reaction at 150 rpm for 1 h at 30 °C. Methanol was removed and washing was performed twice with 10 ml of 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) buffer in the same way as for methanol. After removing the buffer, MA-DVB resin was mixed with 10 ml of E. coli cell-free extract (103 mg of Rcut corresponding to 5670 U) and glutaraldehyde (final concentration 25 mM) and incubated at 4 °C for 20 h with inverting. The immobilization yield was calculated by measuring the amount of the initial protein and the amount of the protein remaining in the supernatant after the immobilization process.

To measure the thermal stability of immRcut, it was treated at various temperature (30–50 °C) for 120 min in 1 ml of 50 mM Tris-HCl pH (8.0). Its residual activity was measured at 30 min interval using pNPC (C8) as substrate at room temperature in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0).

Transesterification reaction was performed using 5 mg of immRcut, 30 μl of ethanol, and pNP-esters (C2–C16) (0.2 mM) in 500 μl of hexane. The reaction was carried out while rotating at 150 rpm for 30 min at 30 °C.

Reaction mixtures were analyzed by HPLC with the same column used to analyze PET degradation products. The elution of the reaction mixture (C2–C8) was performed in a 70:30 ratio of solvent A (acetonitrile) and solvent B (0.1% formic acid) at a flow rate of 1 ml/min at 30 °C. Eluted materials were detected at a UV wavelength of 250 nm. The elution of the reaction mixture (C10–C16) was performed in a solvent A (acetonitrile). Eluted materials were detected under the same conditions. One unit of transesterification activity was defined as 1 μmol of pNP-esters reduced per min.

A bacterial strain (RosL12) having a high lipolytic activity was isolated from the Ross Sea, a deep bay of the Southern Ocean in Antarctica. After the chromosomal DNA of the strain was extracted, 16S rRNA was amplified through PCR. As a result nucleotide sequence analysis (1405 bp, GenBank accession number: OL638143), the sequence was confirmed to be 100% identical to the 16S rRNA sequence of Rhodococcus fascians D188 (GenBank Accession Number: CP015235.1) (Supplementary Fig. S1).

After shotgun cloning was performed using this chromosomal DNA, a transformant E. coli DH5α colony showing the ability to hydrolyze tributyrin (TBN) was discovered in TBN-LB agar medium. The recombinant plasmid, pUC19-Rhod, was extracted from E. coli cells. As a result of performing nucleotide sequencing of the insert DNA, a gene encoding an enzyme that could hydrolyze TBN was discovered. This gene (GenBank accession number OL660765) consisted of 651 bp, encoding 216 amino acids. Its calculated molecular weight was 21,860 Da (Supplementary Fig. S2). We named this enzyme Rcut. Based on NCBI BLAST search, it was most similar to Rhodococcus sp. PBTS2 gene (GenBank Accession Number: CP015220, region 1466525 to 1467175), sharing 98% (639/651 bases) sequence similarities. When the protein sequence of Rcut was searched by BLAST, it was 100% identical to PBAT hydrolase of Rhodococcus sp. (GenBank Accession Number: BCL64964).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Construction of phylogenetic tree and 3D homology structure
ce:section.ce:para: A phylogenetic tree was constructed using amino acid sequences of Rcut and various cutinases deposited in PDB database. Results showed that Rcut was derived from bacteria. However, its amino acid sequences were more similar to amino acid sequences of fungal enzymes than to those of bacterial enzymes (Fig. 1 ).

Fungal cutinases have smaller sizes than most bacterial cutinases. They consist of 5 β-sheet strands inside enzymes and 4–5 α-helices surrounding them [9]. On the other hand, most bacterial cutinases have 9 β-sheet strands and 7 α-helices surrounding them [10].

After confirming that amino acid sequences of Rcut shared 29% sequence identity with those of Fusarium solani cutinase, we constructed a homology model of Rcut using the structure of F. solani cutinase (PDB:1cex) as a template. According to our homology model, Rcut has 5 β-sheet strands and 4 α-helices surrounding the β-sheet (Fig. 2 ). It has a catalytic triad composed of residues S114, H194, and D181 at the active site, with a typical α/β hydrolase fold structure [6]. Cutinase is known to have more than one disulfide bond. Rcut has two disulfide bonds between C32 and C103 and between C177 and C184 at both ends of the protein that might play a very important role in structural stability.

Fungal cutinase is the smallest serine hydrolase, which might help it penetrate the plant's cutin layer [17]. The fact that Rcut is very similar in size and protein sequence to fungal cutinase implicates that the Rhodococcus strain might have received the gene from a fungus, or for some reason it might have evolved in a process similar to fungal cutinase. From this point of view, Rcut is very interesting genetically and evolutionarily.

In order to express Rcut in E. coli, the Rcut gene was subcloned into E. coli expression vector. As a result, pET-Rcut plasmids were constructed. In the case of wild type, enzyme activities of cell free extract (CFE) of E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain were 4.62 U/mg. As a result of SDS-PAGE analysis, it was confirmed that Rcut was produced in insoluble inclusion body forms rather than soluble forms when it was expressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain (arrow 1 in Fig. 3 A). When pET-Rcut plasmids were expressed in E. coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS, enzyme activities of CFEs were increased to 62 U/mg. When pET-pelB-Δ29 plasmid was expressed in E. coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS, enzyme activity of CFE was 61 U/mg. The result of SDS-PAGE analysis of E. coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS (harboring pET-pelB-Δ29 plasmid) confirmed that the Rcut was expressed in soluble forms (arrow 2 in Fig. 3A) unlike Rcut expressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain. As such, it was found that expression levels of Rcut active enzymes were significantly different depending on E. coli host strains. These results seemed to be related to the two disulfide bonds of Rcut. In E. coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS where thioredoxin reductase (trxB) and glutaredoxin reductase (gor) genes have been knocked out, it has been reported that disulfide bonds of foreign proteins are efficiently formed [18]. In addition, F. solani cutinase is water-soluble in E. coli FA113 strain in which the trxB/gor gene is knocked out [19]. The direct relationship between the formation of disulfide bonds in proteins and the formation of soluble enzymes cannot be explained. However, if the disulfide bond is not formed, the protein is expected to be denatured and become aggregated.

Amino acids at positions 1–29 of the N-terminal were predicted as a signal sequence (SS) of Rcut. We prepared two mutants (Δ17 and Δ29) in which parts of the SS were removed and a mutant (pelB-Δ29) in which the SS was replaced with a E. coli pelB SS. These enzymes were expressed with a His-tag attached to the C-terminal. In the case of Δ29 mutant, it was confirmed that the enzyme activity in its CFE was significantly reduced (Fig. 3B). In the case of Δ17 mutant, the enzyme activity was greatly also reduced. On the other hand, when an alternative SS (pelB SS) was attached, it showed a high activity like the WT. These results indicate that the protein has the correct structure and activity only when it passes through the cell membrane using SS and reaches the periplasm.

We expressed Rcut in the form of pelB-Δ29-His in E. coli cells. Mature Rcut was then purified using a Ni-NTA agarose affinity column chromatography and a CM Sepharose column chromatography. SDS-PAGE data for each purification process from the cell free extract were provided in Supplementary Figs. S4 and S5. The purification process was summarized in Table 1 . Finally, the mature Rcut was purified. It had a single protein band (20 kDa) on SDS-PAGE (Fig. 3C). The specific activity of the mature Rcut was 2190 U/mg.

When the substrate specificity of Rcut was investigated, some synthetic fatty acid esters with carbon lengths from 2 to 18 were cleaved (Fig. 4 ). Among them, pNPC (C8) was hydrolyzed the most rapidly. pNPC substrates with medium carbon length (C4–C10) were hydrolyzed relatively well. In general, cutinase prefers substrates with short acyl chains. McCut, a cutinase derived from Malbranchea cinnamomea, has shown high substrate specificity for C4 and C6 substrates [20].

Since Rcut was discovered from a Rhodococcus strain isolated from Antarctica, it was expected to be a psychrophilic enzyme. The optimum temperature was measured to be 40 °C and at temperatures above 50 °C, the activity decreased sharply (Fig. 5 A). Although different substrates were used, PETase also showed the highest activity at 40 °C and the tendency to decrease activity at temperatures higher than 40 °C was similar to that of Rcut [21]. Cold adapted cutinse (TtcutB) derived from Thielavia terrestrissimilarly showed the highest activity at 50 °C, and the activity was rapidly decreased at a temperature higher than 50 °C [22]. Rcut had activities of 65% and 45% at 10 °C and 0 °C, respectively, implying that it could work at a low temperature such as in the Arctic region. The activation energy of Rcut was calculated to be 3.16 kcal/mol in the temperature region from 0 to 40 °C (Fig. 5B), which was very similar to Ea values of typical cold-adapted enzymes [23]. When the Rcut was treated at 50 °C for 10 min, its enzyme activity almost disappeared (data not shown). It was found that its enzyme activity was decreased to 30% after it was treated at 40 °C for 120 min. The enzyme was found to be relatively stable only at temperatures below 30 °C (Fig. 5C).

As a result of investigating pH characteristics of Rcut, it showed the highest activity at pH 9.0. It also showed high activities under alkaline conditions (Fig. 5D). Regarding its pH stability, it showed high stability at pH 4.0–10.0. Its enzyme activity decreased at pH below 4.0 or above 11.0. Temperature and pH characteristics of Rcut were very similar to those of F. solani cutinase [24]. On the other hand, in the case of cutinase TtcutA derived from Thielavia terrestris CAU709, the optimal enzyme activity was shown at pH 4.0 [25].

Effects of various inhibitors, detergents, and metal ions on Rcut were investigated. As shown in Fig. 6 A, the enzyme activity of Rcut was decreased in the presence of 10 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), a well-known inhibitor of serine hydrolase enzyme. β-Mercaptoethanol (BME) and dithiothreitol (DTT) can act as reducing agents to break the disulfide bond. Although Rcut had two disulfide bonds, its activity was not reduced by reducing agents BME or DTT. As Rcut was not affected by EDTA, it could be concluded that metal ions were not required for its enzyme activity or stability.

The stability of Rcut in the presence of detergents was also investigated (Fig. 6B). As a result of the experiment, in the presence of neutral detergent at concentration of 0.5%, the activity of Rcut was not significantly reduced by Tween 20 or Tween 40. However, the activity of Rcut was significantly decreased by Tween 80 and Triton X-100. SDS, an anionic detergent, completely reduced the activity of Rcut. Rcut did not decrease its activity in the presence of most metal ions at a concentration of 5 mM (Fig. 6C). However, its activity was decreased by ZnSO4.

The stability of Rcut was tested in various organic solvents (Fig. 6D). Since various reactions such as esterification and transesterification are carried out in the presence of an organic solvent, high stability in an organic solvent is very important for cutinase [26]. Rcut maintained high enzymatic activities in the presence of various organic solvents such as DMSO, methanol, ethanol, acetone, isopropanol, cyclohexane, and n-hexane at concentrations up to 30% concentration (v/v). Such high stability of Rcut in organic solvents seemed to be related with its cold-adapted property [27]. This stability suggests that this enzyme has the potential to be used in many reactions in organic solvents.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of synthetic polymers by Rcut
ce:section.ce:para: We conducted an experiment to determine whether Rcut could degrade synthetic polymers (PCL, PLA, and PET). PCL film was well decomposed by Rcut. The weight reduction was then measured. PCL film (1 cm2) was decomposed by Rcut at a rate of 76 mg/h/mg Rcut. However, PLA and PET films were hardly decomposed by Rcut (Fig. 7 A). In general, a film-type substrate degradation reaction using enzymes is inefficient because the film substrate has poor accessibility to the enzyme compared to a water-soluble monomer substrate. Nevertheless, the high decomposition rate of Rcut for PCL showed that this enzyme could perform a hydrolysis reaction efficiently because caproic acid ester was a preferred substrate of Rcut.

HPLC analysis was performed to confirm whether Rcut could degrade a PET film. As a result of analyzing the reaction mixture, it was observed that some PET was decomposed by Rcut. Decomposition products of PET were expected to be bis (2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET), mono-(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (MHET), and terephthalate (TPA). Among them, TPA, the final decomposition product and MHET, an intermediate, were detected (Fig. 7B). This result demonstrated that Rcut could degrade PET film into TPA, although the rate of decomposition was not high.

When these three synthetic polymer films treated with Rcut were observed with a scanning electron microscope, the surface structure of the PCL film was clearly deformed and the PLA surface was slightly deformed. However, the surface structure of the PET film did not change at all (Fig. 7C). These results indicate that Rcut could decompose some synthetic polymer films, although the decomposition rate varied greatly depending on the type of material used. In order to efficiently decompose a synthetic polymer film using cutinase, a pretreatment process which increases the accessibility of the film substrate to the enzyme is required.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Immobilization of Rcut and thermal stability assay
ce:section.ce:para: Since the transesterification reaction mainly proceeds in a non-aqueous solvent system, we prepared an immRcut enzyme bound to MA-DVB resin. The immobilization yield was 88.3%. When hydrolysis of pNPC as a substrate with the immRcut was performed, its hydrolytic activity was measured to be 4.09 U/g bead.

Thermal stability of immRcut was also investigated (Fig. 8 A). At 30 °C, it was stable without any activity change for 120 min. After treatment at 40 °C and 50 °C for 120 min, its residual activities were 84% and 52%, respectively. Its free enzyme showed 30% residual activity when it was treated at 40 °C for 120 min. Its free enzyme activity disappeared within 10 min at 50 °C (data not shown). These results indicate that its thermostability can be increased greatly by immobilizing Rcut on the bead.

Transesterification reaction of Rcut was investigated using immRcut (Fig. 8B). When substrates of various carbon lengths were reacted with ethanol, the reaction rate of immRcut was different depending on the chain length. The pNPA with the shortest carbon length showed the highest reaction rate, while the pNPP with the longest carbon length showed the slowest reaction rate. These results confirm that Rcut prefers short-chain fatty acids over long-chain fatty acids when performing a transesterification reaction.

We found a cutinase enzyme from Rhodococcus strain isolated from the Ross Sea. Analysis of its gene sequences revealed that although it was an enzyme derived from bacteria, it was more likely to be fungal enzyme than a bacterial one. This enzyme was expressed as an insoluble form in E. coli BL21 (DE3), although it was expressed as soluble active form in E. coli Rosetta-gami™ 2 (DE3) pLysS in which two reductase genes were knocked out. In addition, its active enzyme was produced only when the signal sequence of its own or other enzyme was included. Rcut was a cold-adapted enzyme. It showed a high activity at alkaline conditions. Among pNP-esters, the substrate with carbon length of C4–C10 was preferred. The most preferred substrate had a carbon length of C8. It showed high stability in various organic solvents. This enzyme rapidly degraded PCL containing ester bond of C6 chain. In addition, it was able to slowly degrade PET containing ester bond of ethylene glycol and terephthalate. ImmRcut showed higher thermal stability than its free enzyme. ImmRcut performed transesterification in a non-polar solvent, suggesting that it could be used for the synthesis of industrially useful ester compounds.
